Title: Passage 1: Small Talk Is Overrated
Content: “I know, it’s so gorgeous outside, but tomorrow it’s supposed to rain.”

So it begins — the conversation that I’ve had `text(one thousand)` times. This kind of inane small talk puts my brain to sleep. Even though small talk is a ritual that is supposed to make talking to strangers and acquaintances easier, it really hinders my ability to connect with other people. It becomes consuming, the way a simple question turns into a `text(five-minute)` conversation about nothing. Small talk has infiltrated every part of my life, too. I found myself asking my great-uncle how work was at the last family gathering. He’s been retired for `text(seven years)`, but the question popped up like a reflex.

Why is small talk so terrible? For me, the problem is that it feels fake and repetitive. We ask questions where the answer is either obvious or trivial, and the answers are practically scripted. The anthropological term for these kinds of conversations is a “phatic expression.” Phatic expressions are meant to create or maintain social relationships, not convey information. So small talk is meaningful because it’s meaningless? That feels backwards. Why not just skip the formalities and have a genuine conversation instead?

I don’t think I’m alone in wanting more interesting conversations. There are `text(hundreds of thousands)` of articles online about how to get better at small talk, which suggests that many people are looking for alternatives. Most social etiquette “experts” will recommend some combination of the following:

:ibox:• Asking your conversation partner questions because people love talking about themselves
• Being an active listener who expresses interest in what your conversation partner says
• Elaborating on your answers so that your conversation partner has more information to respond to

Basically, the experts are recommending that you break the script and get the other person to improvise. This is the secret that these experts don’t want to admit: good conversationalists aren’t having better small talk; they’re turning small talk into meaningful conversations. But to have that kind of conversation, both people need to be willing participants, and not every stranger or acquaintance wants to have a heart-to-heart or an intellectual debate.

There is an alternate solution: companionable silence. So often, we describe silence as “uncomfortable” or “awkward,” but we should embrace these quiet moments instead. Pressure to socially conform has been shown to contribute to stress and anxiety. If we could accept silence as natural, a lot of talking just for the sake of it could be avoided. Sometimes, there just isn’t anything that needs to be said.
